answers.a: Cambodia’s evidence points to two workforce pressures. First, personnel move between the public and private sectors; the government describes recruitment in both directions and notes that individuals may have employment contracts elsewhere. **Inference:** this mobility can make it harder to retain the desired number of civil servants, although the evidence does not quantify turnover or directly identify a retention shortfall. Second, organizational reforms require personnel to be reassigned to match changing needs, with additional training where departments are restructured. The government also directly identifies the quality, efficiency and delivery of public services as continuing challenges. The evidence does not establish specific shortages, pay-related causes or turnover rates.

answers.a: Cambodia’s public-administration reform agenda includes measures that could help retain civil servants, although the cited evidence does not explicitly identify them as a retention strategy. The reforms include raising civil-service pay toward a livable wage, particularly benefiting lower-paid staff; simplifying salary scales and paying salaries electronically and on time; and improving human-resource management through computerisation, pilot performance-management systems and civil-servant training requirements. The agenda also includes institutional rationalisation and restructuring. **Inference:** Better pay, more reliable payment and stronger career-management practices could make civil-service employment more attractive. The cited reform programme covers 2015–2018, so this evidence alone does not establish which measures remain ongoing today.
